title: Inside the Whale and Other Essays
description: Orwell's first collection of essays, published by Victor Gollancz on 11 March 1940 in an edition of 1,100 copies, some of which were later destroyed in German bombing. It has three long essays: 'Charles Dickens', 'Boys' Weeklies' and the title essay, 'Inside the Whale', a review of Henry Miller's Tropic of Cancer that becomes a survey of English writing between the wars.
plot_or_argument: 'Inside the Whale', in three parts, begins as a review of Tropic of Cancer (1934). Orwell values Miller less for his 'unprintable words' than for his writing about the ordinary man, which he compares with Joyce's in Ulysses, and he likens Miller to Whitman as a writer of acceptance rather than of a struggle to change life. He then surveys English writing since the First World War: Housman's nostalgic, adolescent pessimism; the pessimistic, unpolitical writers of the 1920s (Joyce, Eliot, Pound, Lawrence, Wyndham Lewis, Huxley and Strachey); and the serious, left-wing group of the 1930s around Auden and Spender, whose shared public-school and university background and sheltered English lives he blames for their attraction to Communism as a substitute faith, and whose phrase 'necessary murder', in Auden's 'Spain', he says could be written only by someone to whom murder is a word. Finally he takes up Miller's image of Jonah in the whale for a passive acceptance of experience, the last stage of irresponsibility, predicts the break-up of laissez-faire capitalism and liberal-Christian culture, and suggests that any novel worth reading will have to follow Miller's lines. The other two essays, 'Charles Dickens' and 'Boys' Weeklies', were reprinted in Critical Essays (1946), whose record describes them.
narrative_structure: Three essays: 'Charles Dickens', 'Boys' Weeklies' and 'Inside the Whale', the last in three parts.
meter_and_prosody: Discursive critical prose that moves from the review of a single book to a survey of a literary generation and a political argument, quoting Housman and Auden among others and turning on a single governing image, Jonah inside the whale.
historical_context: Orwell had lived in Paris in 1928-29, the city of Miller's book, and dined with Miller there in December 1936 on his way to the Spanish Civil War; Miller thought his going to Spain 'the act of an idiot'. The title essay was finished as the Second World War began: 'While I have been writing this book another European war has broken out.'
literary_significance: Orwell's first book of criticism. The title essay sets literature against the politics of the 1930s, judges the Auden generation as a writer who had himself fought in Spain, and gives its name to the image of the writer inside the whale, passively accepting experience. The collection's other two essays opened Critical Essays (1946), the book that established him as a critic.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eric Arthur Blair. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Victor Gollancz, London, on 11 March 1940 (1,100 copies). A Penguin collection of 1962 with the same title is a different book: a reprint of Selected Essays (1957), keeping 'Inside the Whale' and 'Boys' Weeklies' and adding 'Down the Mine', 'England Your England', 'Shooting an Elephant', 'Lear, Tolstoy and the Fool', 'Politics vs. Literature', 'Politics and the English Language' and 'The Prevention of Literature'.

title: The Lion and the Unicorn
alternative_titles: The Lion and the Unicorn: Socialism and the English Genius
description: Orwell's book-length wartime essay, published by Secker & Warburg on 19 February 1941 as the first of the Searchlight Books, a series edited by T. R. Fyvel and Orwell. It argues that Britain's outdated class system was hampering the war against Nazi Germany, and that only a democratic socialist revolution, at once patriotic and English, could win it.
plot_or_argument: The essay is in three parts: 'England Your England', which opens 'As I write, highly civilized human beings are flying overhead, trying to kill me', 'Shopkeepers at War' and 'The English Revolution'. Orwell argues that the outdated class system is hampering the war effort and that to defeat Nazi Germany Britain needs a socialist revolution, so that being a socialist and a patriot are no longer opposed but complementary. The revolution he proposes would create a democratic 'English Socialism', distinct from the Soviet Communism he regarded as totalitarian, and a new Britishness freed from empire and from the decadent old ruling class; it might keep the royal family as a national symbol while sweeping away the rest of the upper class.
narrative_structure: Three parts: 'England Your England', 'Shopkeepers at War' and 'The English Revolution'. Continuous prose in sections or chapters, the argument or the account advanced from its statement to its conclusion.
literary_form: Essay (published as a book, no. 1 of the Searchlight Books)
meter_and_prosody: Polemical first-person prose that opens under air attack ('As I write, highly civilized human beings are flying overhead, trying to kill me') and proceeds through three titled parts to a programme for an English socialist revolution.
historical_context: Written under air attack, as its opening sentence records, by a writer whose conviction of the dangers of totalitarianism had been formed in the Spanish Civil War. His wife Eileen described its theme as 'how to be a socialist while Tory'.
literary_significance: The essay states without allegory the democratic socialism and hostility to totalitarianism that shape Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, and its first part, 'England Your England', is often treated as an essay in its own right; it later gave its title to a posthumous collection. In a speech on Europe in 1993 the Prime Minister John Major quoted its 'old maids bicycling to Holy Communion through the morning mist'.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Eric Arthur Blair. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Secker & Warburg, London, on 19 February 1941, as no. 1 of the Searchlight Books edited by T. R. Fyvel and Orwell.
